blocks.text: Noah, shut up in the ark, since he had not learned from the raven what he longed to know, namely how far the waters of the flood had decreased, also sent out the dove, a docile bird and friendly to man, which flies long and far, Ps. V, 7. and gladly feeds on the ground, because it is one of the ἐκ τῶν σπερμολόγων [ek tōn spermologōn], and has this implanted in it by its nature, that it returns to its nest from anywhere, even from the most remote places. [col. 28] For these reasons, then, the dove was sent out by Noah; but it returned not long after, because it found no place of rest: for although the tops of the mountains had long since appeared, yet on an earth still λιμναζομένῃ [limnazomenē], as Josephus says, that is, either still standing under water, or at least full of pools and marshy, nothing was then firm. But the same dove, sent out again seven days later, returned toward evening, carrying an olive branch in its mouth. There are some among the Hebrews who will have it that this branch was plucked on the Mount of Olives near Jerusalem, or elsewhere in Judaea, which was untouched by the waters of the flood. Bereshit Rabbah ch. 33: מהיכן הביאה אותו רבי אבא בר כהנא אמר משבשושין שבארץ ישראל הביאה אותו רבי לוי אמר מהר המשחה הביאה אותו דלא טפת ארעה דישראל במבולא והוא שהקבה אומר ליחזקיאל ארץ לא מטוהרה היא ולא גושמה ביום זעם, Whence did it (the dove) bring it (the branch)? Rabbi Abba, son of Cahana (the priest), said: It brought it from the shrubs of the land of Israel. R. Levi said: It brought it from the Mount of Olives, because the land of Israel was not submerged by the flood. As God, the Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Ezekiel in chapter 22, verse 24: That land is not cleansed, nor rained upon in the day of indignation. These things are utterly absurd, since we read that even the highest mountains under the whole heaven were covered by the waters of the flood, Gen. VII, 19. Moreover, to what end would God have kept the land of Canaan, not yet holy, free from the inundation? To what end would he have ordered Noah to build the ark with such great labour? Why was he not rather ordered to withdraw there with the beasts, wild animals and birds? And if the waters of the flood spared the land of Canaan, what became of the inhabitants of that land? Did they too escape the common destruction, and do their descendants, forsooth, acknowledge another ancestor besides Noah, from whom Moses derived the whole human race? And how did God allow the survivors of so great a destruction to be driven out by the accursed Canaan, who not long after the time of the flood seized their dwelling place? Finally, since the waters rose so many cubits above the neighbouring mountains, what prevented them from overwhelming the land of Canaan? They will say this was done by the power of God, and I grant that it could have been done. But although we believe miracles when they are written, still no one is permitted to invent them for himself on his own authority, which these men openly do. For they cite Ezekiel in vain, who has not one γρῦ [gry] about the flood. [II, 561] He only, while reproaching the Israelites with various crimes and recounting the various punishments inflicted, or to be inflicted, on them, denies among other things that their land was, or would be, rained upon in the day of indignation. That is, in keeping with the threats of the Law, Deuter. XI, 17. Lest the Lord, his wrath kindled against you, shut up the heavens, so that there be no rain, and the land yield not its produce. And of the prophet Amos IV, 7., where God speaks thus: I also withheld the rain from you, etc. And I caused it to rain upon one city, and upon another I caused it not to rain: one part was rained upon, and the part on which it did not rain withered. This was shown by a famous example when, at Elijah's word, the heaven was shut, and neither dew nor rain came down upon Judaea for three years and more, 1 Reg. XVII. and XVIII. But we argue in vain, since the very words of Moses amply show that the olive branch was plucked from those places that the flood had inundated. For thus Moses says of Noah, Genes. VIII, 8. He sent forth the dove from him, to see whether the surface of the earth was relieved of the waters. And in verse 11: And the dove came to him in the evening; and behold, a plucked olive leaf in her mouth. And so Noah knew that the surface of the earth was relieved of the waters. This would be falsely said if that leaf had been brought from a land that the flood had not touched. For it could have been brought from there even at the time when the waters elsewhere were at their very highest. From this it also follows that this leaf was not plucked in the earthly Paradise, as others of the Jews assert. Bereshit Rabbah, in the place cited above: רב ביבי אמר [col. 29] נפתחו לה שערי גן עדן והביאה אותו משם, R. Bibi said: The gates of the garden of Eden were opened to it, and from there it brought this leaf. The same opinion is attributed to a certain Berechiah in Vayikra Rabbah at the end of ch. 31. That is, if we believe the Hebrews, the garden of Eden was raised above the highest summits of the mountains, so that the waters of the flood did not reach that far. Many of the ancients incline to the same view. Among them is Lactantius, or rather Venantius, who speaks thus of the earthly Paradise in the poem On the Phoenix,
